candidate.answerReason: The recurrence gives a2=3, a3=6, a6=21, and a12=78.

methods.label: Build only the terms needed
methods.explanation:
The recurrence lets us split an index into any two positive parts. Since \(12=6+6\) and \(6=3+3\), we need only a few earlier terms.

Starting from \(a_1=1\), use the positive index pairs \((1,1)\), \((2,1)\), \((3,3)\), and \((6,6)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_2&=1+1+1\cdot1=3,\\
a_3&=3+1+2\cdot1=6,\\
a_6&=6+6+3\cdot3=21,\\
a_{12}&=21+21+6\cdot6=78.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(a_{12}=\boxed{78}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
methods.levelReason: Substitution into the given recurrence and elementary arithmetic suffice.

methods.label: Find the successive increases
methods.explanation:
Setting one index equal to \(1\) turns the two-index rule into a rule for consecutive terms. For every positive integer \(k\),
\[
a_{k+1}=a_k+a_1+k=a_k+(k+1).
\]
Thus we add \(2\) to reach \(a_2\), then \(3\) to reach \(a_3\), and continue through adding \(12\) to reach \(a_{12}\). Including \(a_1=1\), this gives
\[
a_{12}=1+2+\cdots+12.
\]
Pair the first and last numbers, then the second and next-to-last, and so on. There are six pairs, each with sum \(13\), so
\[
a_{12}=6\cdot13=\boxed{78}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
methods.levelReason: The consecutive-integer sum is evaluated by an elementary pairing argument, without requiring a memorized sequence formula.
